entries.b8b071ecd4e15b7f16a4651f408c5fa0013b3d02: <div sID="gen6121" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="2Sam.9" sID="2Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen6121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6122" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6123" type="x-p"/> The only thing recorded in this chapter is the kindness David showed to Jonathan's seed for his sake. I. The kind enquiry he made after the remains of the house of Saul, and his discovery of Mephibosheth, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The kind reception he gave to Mephibosheth, when he was brought to him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.5-2Sam.9.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. III. The kind provision he made for him and his, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.9-2Sam.9.13">ver. 9-13</reference>.
entries.ad7daad62a9b8da3d6c2b5234df1503b3a143463: <div eID="gen6123" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6122" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Kindness to Jonathan's Son. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1039.)</title> <div sID="gen6124" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake? <hi type="super">2</hi> And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> of the house of Saul a servant whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Ziba. And when they had called him unto David, the king said unto him, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou Ziba? And he said, Thy servant <hi type="italic">is he.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king said, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may shew the kindness of God unto him? And Ziba said unto the king, Jonathan hath yet a son, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> lame on <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the king said unto him, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> he? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lodebar. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then king David sent, and fetched him out of the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, from Lodebar. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now when Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, was come unto David, he fell on his face, and did reverence. And David said, Mephibosheth. And he answered, Behold thy servant! <hi type="super">7</hi> And David said unto him, Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he bowed himself, and said, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I <hi type="italic">am?</hi> <div eID="gen6124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6125" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. David's enquiry after the remains of the ruined house of Saul, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1">v. 1</reference>. This was a great while after his accession to the throne, for it should seem that Mephibosheth, who was but five years old when Saul died, had now a son born, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">v. 12</reference>. David had too long forgotten his obligations to Jonathan, but now, at length, they are brought to his mind. It is good sometimes to bethink ourselves whether there be any promises or engagements that we have neglected to make good; better do it late than never. The compendium which Paul gives us of the life of David is this (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Acts xiii. 36</reference>), that he <hi type="italic">served his generation according to the will of God,</hi> that is, he was a man that made it his business to do good; witness this instance, where we may observe, <div eID="gen6125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6126" type="x-p"/> 1. That he sought an opportunity to do good. He might perhaps have satisfied his conscience with the performance of his promise to Jonathan if he had been only ready, upon request or application made to him by any of his seed, to help and succour them. But he does more, he enquires of those about him first (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1">v. 1</reference>), and, when he met with a person that was likely to inform him, asked him particularly, <hi type="italic">Is there any yet left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.3">v. 3</reference>. "Is there any, not only to whom I may do justice (<reference osisRef="Num.5.8">Num. v. 8</reference>), but to whom I may show kindness?" Note, Good men should seek opportunities of doing good. <hi type="italic">The liberal deviseth liberal things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 8</reference>. For, the most proper objects of our kindness and charity are such as will not be frequently met with without enquiry. The most necessitous are the least clamorous. <div eID="gen6126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6127" type="x-p"/> 2. Those he enquired after were the remains of the house of Saul, to whom he would show kindness for Jonathan's sake: <hi type="italic">Is there any left of the house of Saul?</hi> Saul had a very numerous family (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1 Chron. viii. 33</reference>), enough to replenish a country, and was yet so emptied that none of it appeared; but it was a matter of enquiry, <hi type="italic">Is there any left?</hi> See how the providence of God can empty full families; see how the sin of man will do it. Saul's was a bloody house, no marvel it was thus reduced, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.1">ch. xxi. 1</reference>. But, though God visited the iniquity of the father upon the children, David would not. "Is there any left that I can show kindness to, not for Saul's own sake, but for Jonathan's?" (1.) Saul was David's sworn enemy, and yet he would show kindness to his house with all his heart and was forward to do it. He does not say, "Is there any left of the house of Saul, that I may find some way to take them off, and prevent their giving disturbance to me or my successor?" It was against Abimelech's mind that any one was left of the house of Gideon (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.5">Judg. ix. 5</reference>), and against Athaliah's mind that any one was left of <hi type="italic">the seed royal,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.10-2Chr.22.11">2 Chron. xxii. 10, 11</reference>. Those were usurped governments. David's needed no such vile supports. He was desirous to show kindness to the house of Saul, not only because he trusted in God and feared not what they could do unto him, but because he was of a charitable disposition and forgave what they had done to him. Note, We must evince the sincerity of our forgiving those that have been any way unjust or injurious to us by being ready, as we have opportunity, to show kindness both to them and theirs. We must not only not avenge ourselves upon them, but we must love them, and <hi type="italic">do them good</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Matt. v. 44</reference>), and not be backward to do any office of love and good-will to those that have done us many an injury. <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1 Pet. iii. 9,</reference>—<hi type="italic">but, contrari-wise, blessing.</hi> This is the way to overcome evil, and to find mercy for ourselves and ours, when we or they need it. (2.) Jonathan was David's sworn friend, and therefore he would show kindness to his house. This teaches us, [1.] To be mindful of our covenant. The kindness we have promised we must conscientiously perform, though it should not be claimed. God is faithful to us; let us not be unfaithful to one another. [2.] To be mindful of our friendships, our old friendships. Note, Kindness to our friends, even to them and theirs, is one of the laws of our holy religion. <hi type="italic">He that has friends must show himself friendly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">Prov. xviii. 24</reference>. If Providence has raised us, and our friends and their families are brought low, yet we must not forget former acquaintance, but rather look upon that as giving us so much the fairer opportunity of being kind to them: then our friends have most need of us and we are in the best capacity to help them. Though there be not a solemn league of friendship tying us to this constancy of love, yet there is a sacred law of friendship no less obliging, that to him that is in misery pity should be shown by his friend, <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job vi. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">A brother is born for adversity.</hi> Friendship obliges us to take cognizance of the families and surviving relations of those we have loved, who, when they left us, left behind them their bodies, their names, and their posterity, to be kind to. <div eID="gen6127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6128" type="x-p"/> 3. The kindness he promised to show them he calls the <hi type="italic">kindness of God;</hi> not only great kindness, but, (1.) Kindness in pursuance of the covenant that was between him and Jonathan, to which God was a witness. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.42">1 Sam. xx. 42</reference>. (2.) Kindness after God's example; for we must be merciful as he is. He spares those whom he has advantage against, and so must we. Jonathan's request to David was (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14-1Sam.20.15">1 Sam. xx. 14, 15</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Show me the kindness of the Lord, that I die not,</hi> and the same to my seed." The kindness of God is some greater instance of kindness than one can ordinarily expect from men. (3.) It is kindness done after a godly sort, and with an eye to God, and his honour and favour. <div eID="gen6128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6129" type="x-p"/> II. Information given him concerning Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan. Ziba was an old retainer to Saul's family, and knew the state of it. He was sent for and examined, and informed the king that Jonathan's son was living, but <hi type="italic">lame</hi> (how he came to be so we read before, <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">ch. iv. 4</reference>), and that he lived in obscurity, probably among his mother's relations in Lo-debar in Gilead, on the other side Jordan, where he was <hi type="italic">forgotten, as a dead man out of mind,</hi> but bore this obscurity the more easily because he could remember little of the honour he fell from. <div eID="gen6129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6130" type="x-p"/> III. The bringing of him to court. The king sent (Ziba, it is likely) to bring him up to Jerusalem with all convenient speed, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.5">v. 5</reference>. Thus he eased Machir of his trouble, and perhaps recompensed him for what he had laid out on Mephibosheth's account. This Machir appears to have been a very generous free-hearted man, and to have entertained Mephibosheth, not out of any disaffection to David or his government, but in compassion to the reduced son of a prince, for afterwards we find him kind to David himself when he fled from Absalom. He is named (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.27">ch. xvii. 27</reference>) among those that furnished the king with what he wanted at Mahanaim, though David, when he sent for Mephibosheth from him, little thought that the time would come when he himself would gladly be beholden to him: and perhaps Machir was then the more ready to help David in recompence for his kindness to Mephibosheth. Therefore we should be forward to give, because we know not but we ourselves may some time be in want, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Eccl. xi. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">And he that watereth shall be watered also himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.25">Prov. xi. 25</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen6130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6131" type="x-p"/> 1. Mephibosheth presented himself to David with all the respect that was due to his character. Lame as he was, <hi type="italic">he fell on his face, and did homage,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.6">v. 6</reference>. David had thus made his honours to Mephibosheth's father, Jonathan, when he was next to the throne (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1 Sam. xx. 41</reference>, <hi type="italic">he bowed himself to him three times</hi>), and now Mephibosheth, in like manner, addresses him, when affairs are so completely reversed. Those who, when they are in inferior relations, show respect, shall, when they come to be advanced, have respect shown to them. <div eID="gen6131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6132" type="x-p"/> 2. David received him with all the kindness that could be. (1.) He spoke to him as one surprised, but pleased to see him. "Mephibosheth! Why, is there such a man living?" He remembered his name, for it is probable that he was born about the time of the intimacy between him and Jonathan. (2.) He bade him not be afraid: <hi type="italic">Fear not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7">v. 7</reference>. It is probable that the sight of David put him into some confusion, to free him from which he assures him that he sent for him, not out of any jealousy he had of him, nor with any bad design upon him, but to show him kindness. Great men should not take a pleasure in the timorous approaches of their inferiors (for the great God does not), but should encourage them. (3.) He gives him, by grant from the crown, <hi type="italic">all the land of Saul his father,</hi> that is, his paternal estate, which was forfeited by Ishbosheth's rebellion and added to his own revenue. This was a real favour, and more than giving him a kind word. True friendship will be generous. (4.) Though he had thus given him a good estate, sufficient to maintain him, yet for Jonathan's sake (whom perhaps he saw some resemblance of in Mephibosheth's face), he will take him to be a constant guest at his own table, where he will not only be comfortably fed, but have company and attendance suitable to his birth and quality. Though Mephibosheth was lame and unsightly, and does not appear to have had any great fitness for business, yet, for his good father's sake, David took him to be one of his family. <div eID="gen6132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6133" type="x-p"/> 3. Mephibosheth accepts this kindness with great humility and self-abasement. He was not one of those that take every favour as a debt, and think every thing too little that their friends do for them; but, on the contrary, speaks as one amazed at the grants David made him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is thy servant, that thou shouldst look upon such a dead dog as I am?</hi> How does he vilify himself! Though the son of a prince, and the grandson of a king, yet his family being under guilt and wrath, and himself poor and lame, he calls himself <hi type="italic">a dead dog</hi> before David. Note, It is good to have the heart humble under humbling providences. If, when divine Providence brings our condition down, divine grace brings our spirits down with it, we shall be easy. And those who thus humble themselves shall be exalted. How does he magnify David's kindness! It would have been easy to lessen it if he had been so disposed. Had David restored him his father's estate? It was but giving him his own. Did he take him to his table? This was policy, that he might have an eye upon him. But Mephibosheth considered all that David said and did as very kind, and himself as less than the least of all his favours. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">1 Sam. xviii. 18</reference>.
entries.3f53dd881cd8b48e1d275a71034f524982908f91: <div eID="gen6133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Then the king called to Ziba, Saul's servant, and said unto him, I have given unto thy master's son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him, and thou shalt bring in <hi type="italic">the fruits,</hi> that thy master's son may have food to eat: but Mephibosheth thy master's son shall eat bread alway at my table. Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said Ziba unto the king, According to all that my lord the king hath commanded his servant, so shall thy servant do. As for Mephibosheth, <hi type="italic">said the king,</hi> he shall eat at my table, as one of the king's sons. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Micha. And all that dwelt in the house of Ziba <hi type="italic">were</hi> servants unto Mephibosheth. <hi type="super">13</hi> So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet. <div eID="gen6134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6135" type="x-p"/> The matter is here settled concerning Mephibosheth. 1. This grant of his father's estate is confirmed to him, and Ziba called to be a witness to it (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.9">v. 9</reference>); and, it should seem, Saul had a very good estate, for his father was a mighty man of substance (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1 Sam. ix. 1</reference>), and he had fields and vineyards to bestow, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7">1 Sam. xxii. 7</reference>. Be it ever so much, Mephibosheth is now master of it all. 2. The management of the estate is committed to Ziba, who knew what it was and how to make the most of it, in whom, having been his father's servant, he might confide, and who, having a numerous family of sons and servants, had hands sufficient to be employed about it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">v. 10</reference>. Thus Mephibosheth is made very easy, having a good estate without care, and is in a fair way of being very rich, having much coming in and little occasion to spend, himself being kept at David's table. Yet he must have food to eat besides his own bread, provisions for his son and servants; and Ziba's sons and servants would come in for their share of his revenue, for which reason perhaps their number is here mentioned, <hi type="italic">fifteen sons and twenty servants,</hi> who would require nearly all there was; <hi type="italic">for as goods are increased those are increased that eat them, and what good has the owner thereof save the beholding of them with his eyes?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Eccl. v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">All that dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants to Mephibosheth</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">v. 12</reference>), that is, they all lived upon him, and made a prey of his estate, under pretence of waiting on him and doing him service. The Jews have a saying, "He that multiplies servants multiplies thieves." Ziba is now pleased, for he loves wealth, and will have abundance. "As <hi type="italic">the king has commanded, so will thy servant do,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.11">v. 11</reference>. Let me alone with the estate: and <hi type="italic">as for Mephibosheth</hi>" (they seem to be Ziba's words), "if the king please, he need not trouble the court, <hi type="italic">he shall eat at my table,</hi> and be as well treated <hi type="italic">as one of the king's sons.</hi>" But David will have him at his own table, and Mephibosheth is as well pleased with his post as Ziba with his. How unfaithful Ziba was to him we shall find afterwards, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.3">ch. xvi. 3</reference>. Now because David was a type of Christ, his Lord and son, his root and offspring, let his kindness to Mephibosheth serve to illustrate the kindness and love of God our Saviour towards fallen man, which yet he was under no obligation to, as David was to Jonathan. Man was convicted of rebellion against God, and, like Saul's house, under a sentence of rejection from him, was not only brought low and impoverished, but lame and impotent, made so by the fall. The Son of God enquires after this degenerate race, that enquired not after him, comes to seek and save them. To those of them that humble themselves before him, and commit themselves to him, he restores the forfeited inheritance, he entitles them to a better paradise than that which Adam lost, and takes them into communion with himself, sets them with his children at his table, and feasts them with the dainties of heaven. <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man, that thou shouldst thus magnify him!</hi>  <chapter eID="2Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen6135" type="x-p"/>

entries.a8eb58c6a7bc59d9fd13b4d2df74ec82cd21b623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2901"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <div sID="gen3997" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.12">2Sa 9:1-12</reference>. David Sends for Mephibosheth.<div eID="gen3997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2901"/><hi type="bold">1-7. David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul--</hi>On inquiry, Saul's land steward was found, who gave information that there still survived Mephibosheth, a son of Jonathan who was five years old at his father's death, and whom David, then wandering in exile, had never seen. His lameness (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>) had prevented him from taking any part in the public contests of the time. Besides, according to Oriental notions, the younger son of a crowned monarch has a preferable claim to the succession over the son of a mere heir-apparent; and hence his name was never heard of as the rival of his uncle Ish-bosheth. His insignificance had led to his being lost sight of, and it was only through Ziba that David learned of his existence, and the retired life he passed with one of the great families in trans-jordanic Canaan who remained attached to the fallen dynasty. Mephibosheth was invited to court, and a place at the royal table on public days was assigned him, as is still the custom with Eastern monarchs. Saul's family estate, which had fallen to David in right of his wife (<reference osisRef="Num.27.8">Nu 27:8</reference>), or been forfeited to the crown by Ish-bosheth's rebellion (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.8">2Sa 12:8</reference>), was provided (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.11">2Sa 9:11</reference>; also <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.28">2Sa 19:28</reference>), for enabling Mephibosheth to maintain an establishment suitable to his rank, and Ziba appointed steward to manage it, on the condition of receiving one-half of the produce in remuneration for his labor and expense, while the other moiety was to be paid as rent to the owner of the land (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">2Sa 19:29</reference>). <div eID="gen3998" type="x-p"/>
entries.69d2e19b694b4aeec8fcb361390e9ec60c8c6ae8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2902"/><div sID="gen3999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2902"/><hi type="bold">10. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants--</hi>The mention of his sons and the slaves in his house was to show that Mephibosheth would be honored with an equipage "as one of the king's sons." <div eID="gen3999" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c79d2f291a3ed0572f9995bdc9acd5bb68d3aab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2903"/><div sID="gen4000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2903"/><hi type="bold">12. Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Micah--</hi>Whether born before or after his residence in Jerusalem, cannot be ascertained. But through him the name and memory of the excellent Jonathan was preserved (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.34">1Ch 8:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.40">9:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.41">41</reference>). <chapter eID="2Sam.9"/>

entries.d6bf7f9464e6b720edfe51ba52b95cf084667107: <div eID="gen10898" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10899" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10900" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10900" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10899" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10901" type="x-p"/> David inquires after the family of Jonathan, and is informed of Mephibosheth his son, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.4">2Sam 9:1-4</reference>. He sends for him and gives him all the land of Saul, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.5-2Sam.9.8">2Sam 9:5-8</reference>; and appoints Ziba the servant of Saul, and his family, to till the ground for Mephibosheth, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.9-2Sam.9.13">2Sam 9:9-13</reference>. <div eID="gen10901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10903" type="x-p"/> Is there yet any that is left - David recollecting the covenant made with his friend Jonathan, now inquires after his family. It is supposed that political considerations prevented him from doing this sooner. Reasons of state often destroy all the charities of life.
entries.dd5f2a111ea898dac45625e605702f0166931e60: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10904" type="x-p"/> That I may show the kindness of God unto him? - That is, the utmost, the highest degrees of kindness; as the hail of God, is very great hail, the mountains of God, exceeding high mountains: besides, this kindness was according to the covenant of God made between him and the family of Jonathan.
entries.5e8baf4f3cd5744f2ccabae4d028358d882b49dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10905" type="x-p"/> Lo-debar - Supposed to have been situated beyond Jordan; but there is nothing certain known concerning it.
entries.086a301c00ed8c01f3ae2aebde2f7221c16ec2c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10906" type="x-p"/> Will restore thee all the land - I believe this means the mere family estate of the house of Kish, which David as king might have retained, but which most certainly belonged, according to the Israelitish law, to the descendants of the family. <div eID="gen10906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10907" type="x-p"/> And thou shalt eat bread at my table - This was kindness, (the giving up the land was justice), and it was the highest honor that any subject could enjoy, as we may see from the reference made to it by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Luk.22.30">Luk 22:30</reference> (note): That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom. For such a person David could do no more. His lameness rendered him unfit for any public employment.
entries.8b0adf8807bacb9d1051999f10055cd18afbf032: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10908" type="x-p"/> I have given unto thy master's son - Unless Ziba had been servant of Jonathan, this seems to refer to Micha, son of Mephibosheth, and so some understand it; but it is more likely that Mephibosheth is meant, who is called son of Saul instead of grandson. Yet it is evident enough that the produce of the land went to the support of Micha, (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">2Sam 9:10</reference>), for the father was provided for at the table of David; but all the patrimony belonged to Mephibosheth.
entries.adc5906f8fc5bcfc5f42f6acad6e411662866b0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10909" type="x-p"/> Thou therefore, and thy sons - shall till the land - It seems that Ziba and his family had the care of the whole estate, and cultivated it at their own expense, yielding the half of the produce to the family of Mephibosheth. Ziba was properly the hind, whose duty and interest it was to take proper care of the ground, for the better it was cultivated the more it produced; and his half would consequently be the greater.
entries.bd0f04b7fc7c05325dd204a55cc37c72dc42ff55: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10910" type="x-p"/> So shall thy servant do - The promises of Ziba were fair and specious, but he was a traitor in his heart, as we shall see in the rebellion of Absalom, and David's indulgence to this man is a blot in his character; at this time however he suspected no evil; circumstances alone can develope the human character. The internal villain can be known only when circumstances occur which can call his propensities into action; till then he may be reputed an honest man.
entries.0ce8b1ec043e35926b222e6de06fa1ecb39dd7f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10911" type="x-p"/> Did eat continually at the king's table - He was fit for no public office, but was treated by the king with the utmost respect and affection.  <chapter eID="2Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen10911" type="x-p"/>

entries.7502984391bb22cde0e4de6339a805d630fc113a: <div eID="gen4348" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">David’s Kindness towards Mephibosheth - <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:1-13</reference></title> <div sID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> When David was exalted to be king over all Israel, he sought to show compassion to the house of the fallen king, and to repay the love which his noble-minded friend Jonathan had once sworn to him before the Lord (1Sa 20:13.; comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.17-2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:17-18</reference>). The account of this forms the conclusion of, or rather an appendix to, the first section of the history of his reign, and was intended to show how David was mindful of the duty of gratitude and loving fidelity, even when he reached the highest point of his regal authority and glory. The date when this occurred was about the middle of David’s reign, as we may see from the fact, that Mephibosheth, who was five years old when Saul died (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>), had a young son at the time (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">2Sa 9:12</reference>). <div eID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.1-2Sam.9.4">2Sa 9:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> When David inquired whether there was any one left of the house of Saul to whom he could show favour for Jonathan’s sake (ישׁ־עוד הכי: <hi type="italic">is it so that there is any one?</hi> = there is certainly some one left), a servant of Saul named <hi type="italic">Ziba</hi> was summoned, who told the king that there was a son of Jonathan living in the house of Machir at Lodebar, and that he was lame in his feet. אישׁ עוד האפס, <hi type="italic">“is there no one at all besides?”</hi> The ל before בּית is a roundabout way of expressing the genitive, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.18">1Sa 16:18</reference>, etc., and is obviously not to be altered into מבּית, as Thenius proposes. <hi type="italic">“The kindness of God”</hi> is love and kindness shown in God, and for God’s sake (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.36">Luk 6:36</reference>). <hi type="italic">Machir</hi> the son of Ammiel was a rich man, judging from <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.27">2Sa 17:27</reference>, who, after the death of Saul and Jonathan, had received the lame son of the latter into his house. <hi type="italic">Lodebar</hi> (לודבר, written לאדבר in <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.27">2Sa 17:27</reference>, but erroneously divided by the Masoretes into two words in both passages) was a town on the east of Mahanaim, towards Rabbath Amman, probably the same place as Lidbir (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.26">Jos 13:26</reference>); but it is not further known.
entries.ccf01bbb5b9befb2d116b1f3140d32e5e8c529dd: <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.5-2Sam.9.7">2Sa 9:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> David sent for this son of Jonathan (<hi type="italic">Mephibosheth</hi>: cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>), and not only restored his father’s possessions in land, but took him to his own royal table for the rest of his life. <hi type="italic">“Fear not,”</hi> said David to Mephibosheth, when he came before him with the deepest obeisance, to take away any anxiety lest the king should intend to slay the descendants of the fallen king, according to the custom of eastern usurpers. It is evident from the words, <hi type="italic">“I will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father,”</hi> that the landed property belonging to Saul had either fallen to David as crown lands, or had been taken possession of by distant relations after the death of Saul. <hi type="italic">“Thou shalt eat bread at my table continually,”</hi> i.e., eat at my table all thy life long, or receive thy food from my table.
entries.94d561bf5c8a202cb8f24b051baad4ad5e625730: <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.8">2Sa 9:8</reference> <div eID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> Mephibosheth expressed his thanks for this manifestation of favour with the deepest obeisance, and a confession of his unworthiness of any such favour. On his comparison of himself to a <hi type="italic">“dead dog,”</hi> see at 1Sa 24:15.
entries.26c6798abc2b662e5f53ad6a031929f9301c3505: <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.9-2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4354" type="x-p"/> David then summoned Ziba the servant of Saul, told him of the restoration of Saul’s possessions to his son Mephibosheth, and ordered him, with his sons and servants, to cultivate the land for the son of his lord. The words, <hi type="italic">“that thy master’s son may have food to eat,”</hi> are not at variance with the next clause, <hi type="italic">“Mephibosheth shall eat bread alway at my table,”</hi> as bread is a general expression, including all the necessaries of life. Although Mephibosheth himself ate daily as a guest at the king’s table, he had to make provision as a royal prince for the maintenance of his own family and servants, as he had children according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">2Sa 9:12</reference> and 1Ch 8:34. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:10</reference>), with whom he had probably been living in Gibeah, Saul’s native place, and may perhaps have hitherto farmed Saul’s land.
entries.ed48b50610eab0b0c06ddf06dd863353d671521e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.11-2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen4354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> Ziba promised to obey the king’s command. The last clause of this verse is a circumstantial clause in form, with which the writer passes over to the conclusion of his account. But the words שׁלחני על שׁלחן, <hi type="italic">“at my table,”</hi> do not tally with this, as they require that the words should be taken as David’s own. This is precluded, however, not only by the omission of any intimation that David spoke again after Ziba, and repeated what he had said once already, and that without any occasion whatever, but also by the form of the sentence, more especially the participle אכל. There is no other course left, therefore, than to regard שׁלחני (my table) as written by mistake for דּוד שׁלחן: <hi type="italic">“but Mephibosheth ate at David’s table as one of the king’s sons.”</hi> The further notices in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">2Sa 9:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:13</reference> follow this in a very simple manner. בּית מושׁב כּל, <hi type="italic">“all the dwelling,”</hi> i.e., all the inhabitants of Ziba’s house, namely his sons and servants, were servants of Mephibosheth, i.e., worked for him and cultivated his land, whilst he himself took up his abode at Jerusalem, to eat daily at the king’s table, although he was lamed in both his feet.  <chapter eID="2Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen4355" type="x-p"/>

entries.8c7e69b42d705a034459b12077d75ad4b1ba9d65:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="9" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND David said <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Wars being ended, he set himself to the Admini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration of Justice to all his People, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 15. And a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst others he minds his just debt and obligation to <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nathan</ns0:hi> and his Family.</ns0:note>, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He saith not <ns0:hi>of the house of Iona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />than,</ns0:hi> for he knew not of any Son which he had left, and therefore thought his kindness and obligation was to pass to the next of his Kindred. As for <ns0:hi>Mephibosheth,</ns0:hi> he was ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry young and obscure, and possibly concealed by his Friends, lest <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should cut him off from jealousie of State, as hath been usual among Princes in like case, and therefore was unknown to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> as well he might be, especially when <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s head and hands were full of War with divers and Potent Enemies, as they had hitherto been.</ns0:note>, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathans sake?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> of the house of Saul a servant <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">One who had been a Servant, and, as it may seem, a Stew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ard to <ns0:hi>Saul.</ns0:hi> See below, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10.</ns0:note> whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 1. & 19. 29.</ns0:note> Ziba: and when they had cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led him unto David, the king said unto him, <ns0:hi>Art</ns0:hi> thou Ziba? And he said, Thy servant <ns0:hi>is he.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the king said, <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may shew the kindness of God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either, First, That kindness which I owe him for Gods sake, and by vertue of my Oath given to him about it, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 14, 15. But that Oath seems onely to oblige him to <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi>'s Posterity, and not to any other of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s House. Or, Secondly, Great and eminent kindness.</ns0:note> unto him? And Ziba said unto the king, Jonathan hath yet a son, <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4. 4.</ns0:note> lame on his feet.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And the king said unto him, Where <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lode<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bar <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">In a place beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan, chap.</ns0:hi> 17. 27. where his Friends thought he might be kept out of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s sight.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 ¶ Then king David sent, and fet him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />debar.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Now when Mephibosheth the son of Jona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />than, the son of Saul, was come unto David, he fell on his face, and did reverence: And David said, Mephibosheth. And he answered, Behold thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 ¶ And David said unto him, Fear not; for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy fathers sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which were now seized and possessed by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> as due to him, either, in right of his Wife, to whom the Inheritance was devolved, <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Sons by his Wives being all dead. See <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 27. 8. or, by Divine Donation, as belonging to the Crown which God had now given him: or, by forfeiture, because of <ns0:hi>Ishbosheth</ns0:hi>'s Rebellion against his Lord and King.</ns0:note>, and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And he bowed himself, and said, What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 24. 14.</ns0:note> dead dog as I <ns0:hi>am?</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>g</ns0:hi> So contemptible in my person and condition.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ Then the king called to Ziba Sauls ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant, and said unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Chap. 19. 29.</ns0:note> I have given unto thy masters son all that pertained to Saul, and to all his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants shall till the land for him, and thou shalt bring in <ns0:hi>the fruits,</ns0:hi> that thy masters son may have food to eat <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That he may have wherewith to buy Food for all his Family, and all manner of provisions (which oft come under the tile of <ns0:hi>Food</ns0:hi> and Bread) necessary for himself and them.</ns0:note>: but Mephibosheth thy masters son shall eat bread alway at my table. Now Ziba had fifteen sons, and twenty servants <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For it is probable he had been the chief Steward to manage <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Lands: whereby he had great opportuni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties to inrich himself, which also he was very intent and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solved upon, either directly, or indirectly, as the following History of him shews; and therefore it is not strange that he was so rich.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then said Ziba unto the king, According to all that my lord the king hath commanded his servant, so shall thy servant do. As for Mephibo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sheth, <ns0:hi>said the king,</ns0:hi> he shall eat at my table, as one of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ings sons <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">These are the words, Either, First, Of <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> the words, <ns0:hi>said he,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>said the King,</ns0:hi> being supplied out of the former and following Verses. Or, Secondly, Of <ns0:hi>Ziba,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing thus rendred and understood, <ns0:hi>Also Mephibosheth,</ns0:hi> if the King so please, <ns0:hi>shall eat at my table,</ns0:hi> and shall be treated there according to his Quality<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>as one of thy Sons,</ns0:hi> as thou desirest: for the Estate will suffice for that also.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Mephibosheth had a young son <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either, First, Before he was discovered and brought to the King; and then <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> seems guilty of a great error in forgetting his dear <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> so long; although his long and continued Wars both Civil and Foreign, might afford him some excuse, as filling his mind and time with business of another nature. Or, Secondly, After that time: for there is nothing here which determines when this Son was Born.</ns0:note>, whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Micha <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who also had other Children and Grand-Children, to keep up the name and memory of worthy and famous <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nathan.</ns0:hi> See 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 8. 34, 35. and 9. 40, 41.</ns0:note>: and all that dwelt in the house of Ziba <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> servants unto Mephibosheth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:254" />
he did eat continually at the kings table; and was lame on both his feet.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
